name: Handshake
baseMeaning: Two hands clasped together, one reaching in from each side — marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce.
tldr: The handshake emoji 🤝 reads as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: two hands clasped together, one reaching in from each side. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Closing a deal with a client 🤝

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce.
contextMeanings.example: Signalling a truce after a group argument 🤝

platformNotes.note: On Instagram 🤝 usually arrives as the tail of a caption rather than as a post of its own — a sign-off that reads as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce under a photo, or a reaction somebody left on a story.

In TikTok comments 🤝 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🤝 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for closing a deal with a client, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🤝 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🤝 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like signalling a truce after a group argument. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

generationalNotes.note: Gen X mostly uses 🤝 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🤝 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for 🤝 to do the work of closing a deal with a client, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce.

Millennials tend to send 🤝 deliberately, usually for something like signalling a truce after a group argument, and they read marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce into it more often than the older cohorts do.

warnings.description: The Briefcase 💼 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the handshake closes the deal in the air, the briefcase stands for the contract and the money behind it. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🤝 as something else fairly often: it gets assumed to mean the parties are close, when most often it just closes a negotiation without ceremony — in group chats it is also used to end an argument rather than celebrate one. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: What Does the Handshake Emoji 🤝 Mean? A Full Breakdown
seoDescription: The meaning of 🤝 Handshake in texts and DMs, with the handshake readings, the common misread, and the pickers it gets confused with.

longForm.overview:
This page is the untoned drawing. Somewhere below it are five versions of the same handshake with a skin tone applied, and those pages are about something different: not what the gesture means, but what a particular tone adds to it when it arrives from a particular face.

The short version. The handshake is for closing a deal with a client and for signalling a truce after a group argument, it gets misread often enough to be worth writing down, and it has five skin-tone versions worth reading on their own. The sections below take those in turn.

Unicode 13.0 is where 🤝 comes from. The drawing shows two hands clasped together, one reaching in from each side, it sits in the hand-fingers-partial group of the set, and in a conversation it does one thing: it says what a sentence would have said less well.

What it says is marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — the picture does the same work as the words it replaces, and it gets there faster.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets assumed to mean the parties are close, when most often it just closes a negotiation without ceremony — in group chats it is also used to end an argument rather than celebrate one. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 💼 Briefcase: the handshake closes the deal in the air, the briefcase stands for the contract and the money behind it. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
There is one habit that turns a small emoji into a misunderstanding. 🤝 goes back on its own, with no words around it, and it stands for whatever the sender had in mind — which was marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce. The reader gets the drawing and none of the context that produced it.

Start with Closing a deal with a client. That is where the handshake earns its place: it closes a sentence that has already said the thing, and nobody has to add "you know what I mean". The other job is signalling a truce after a group argument, and there the emoji is not the message but the temperature of the message.

The setting does half the work. 🤝 used for closing a deal with a client in a work channel reads as a handover; the same move in a group chat reads as a joke. The emoji is not saying anything different — the audience is.

Which is also why this family has skin-tone pages. The gesture is the same in all five, and the tone you choose is the only part of the message that says anything about you.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
There is also a place where this emoji does not belong: the professional setting. 🤝 under a review, or in a first message to a client, reads as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, and in that room the same reading sounds like somebody settling a point.

Two rules. First, 💼 Briefcase is a different message: the handshake closes the deal in the air, the briefcase stands for the contract and the money behind it. Do not send 🤝 when you meant that one. Second, a reaction to bad news needs words. A bare 🤝 reads as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, and nobody in a thread about a person wants to be answered with a drawing of a gesture.

Not every message survives being turned into a picture. The emoji gets assumed to mean the parties are close, when most often it just closes a negotiation without ceremony — in group chats it is also used to end an argument rather than celebrate one, and the sentence underneath it loses the argument. Once 🤝 is carrying the meaning, the meaning has moved without either sender moving it.

With somebody you have just met, it is worse. 🤝 has no warmth in the drawing, and the gesture has picked up an edge of superiority from being used to answer other people.
longForm.howToReply:
If the intent is warmth, the sentence is the part that carries it. Sending 🤝 next to a message like closing a deal with a client leaves the reader to guess whether it was marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce or something sharper.

If it was a reaction, 🤝 back is a complete answer. It says "same" without writing a word, and the exchange can end there.

If it was aimed at you, it needs text. 🤝 replying to 🤝 looks like a conversation between two drawings, and whatever the sender actually asked never gets answered.

When the register is unclear, the words win. The drawing gets assumed to mean the parties are close, when most often it just closes a negotiation without ceremony — in group chats it is also used to end an argument rather than celebrate one, so the sentence it was sent with is the only reliable guide to what it meant.

faqs.question: Is 🤝 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, but it gets assumed to mean the parties are close, when most often it just closes a negotiation without ceremony — in group chats it is also used to end an argument rather than celebrate one. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🤝 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤝 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under handshake show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🤝 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🤝 is used for marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce. The drawing shows two hands clasped together, one reaching in from each side, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤝 and 💼?
faqs.answer: The handshake closes the deal in the air, the briefcase stands for the contract and the money behind it. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🤝
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets assumed to mean the parties are close, when most often it just closes a negotiation without ceremony — in group chats it is also used to end an argument rather than celebrate one more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: closing a deal with a client 🤝
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: closing a deal with a client 🤝
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: signalling a truce after a group argument 🤝
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as marking a deal, an agreement, or a truce, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.
